hypotheses.claim: Changing `matches(String)` to `matches(String...)` removes the JVM-level `matches(String)` method, so previously compiled plugins or modules invoking that public method may fail at runtime with `NoSuchMethodError`.
hypotheses.why_suspected: Java varargs compile as an array parameter, changing the descriptor from `(String)` to `(String[])`; the evidence shows direct replacement rather than retaining a forwarding single-name overload.
questions_to_resolve: Is `DBSObjectFilter` part of the binary compatibility contract for independently compiled DBeaver plugins?
Are any distributed or third-party binaries compiled against `matches(String)`?

hypotheses.claim: Multi-name filtering may reject an overloaded object even when one candidate identity satisfies the complete filter, because inclusion matching one name and exclusion matching a different name is evaluated as a rejection rather than evaluating each candidate identity independently.
hypotheses.why_suspected: The implementation computes `any name matches an include` and then rejects on `any name matches an exclude`. Thus, for example, an overloaded name can satisfy the include while the ordinary name independently satisfies an exclude, although the included identity itself is not excluded.
questions_to_resolve: Is the intended contract `exists name: include(name) && !exclude(name)`, or should an exclusion matching any alias reject the whole object?
What results are expected when include and exclude patterns match different identities of the same overloaded object?

outcomes.supported_claim: A pre-change binary of the separate `org.jkiss.dbeaver.erd.model` plugin containing `DiagramObjectCollector.collectTables` is binary-incompatible with the changed `DBSObjectFilter`; if that call path executes against the new class, method resolution can fail with `NoSuchMethodError` for `matches(String)`.
outcomes.reasoning: The diff replaces the public one-argument method with a varargs method. Although source calls with one `String` still compile, `String...` has the JVM descriptor `String[]`, not `String`; it does not preserve the old method descriptor. E15 shows a caller in another plugin making the one-argument call, and L2 shows that the containing package is exported. A binary of that caller compiled before the change references `matches(Ljava/lang/String;)Z`, while the changed class supplies `matches([Ljava/lang/String;)Z`.
outcomes.causal_link: The changed declaration removes the `matches(String)` JVM method and introduces `matches(String[])`. Therefore an unchanged, previously compiled cross-plugin invocation targeting the former descriptor cannot resolve against the new class and can throw `NoSuchMethodError` when executed.

outcomes.supported_claim: For overloaded objects filtered in DBNDatabaseNode, the change supplies both the ordinary name and overloaded name; DBSObjectFilter then allows an include pattern to match either supplied name and rejects the object if an exclude pattern matches either supplied name, including a different name from the include match.
outcomes.reasoning: The cross-identity rejection mechanism is established: inclusion and exclusion independently search all supplied names, and an exclusion match returns false. The navigator change exposes overloaded objects to this behavior by passing both getName() and getOverloadedName(). However, the evidence does not establish that this behavior violates the intended filter contract. E25 explicitly notes uncertainty about the overloaded identity and user expectations, and L6 provides no relevant test evidence. There is also no concrete evidence that the two names differ for an actual overloaded object on this path. Therefore the changed behavior is established, but the alleged defect is not.
outcomes.causal_link: Previously this navigator path called matches only with the ordinary object name. The changed DBNDatabaseNode call supplies two names for DBPOverloadedObject instances, while the changed DBSObjectFilter evaluates include and exclude patterns independently across the entire name array. Consequently, if one supplied name matches an include and another matches an exclude, the new path returns false. Whether that newly exposed result is erroneous cannot be determined from the supplied evidence.
